articles.title: Taylor Swift and Dolly Parton recorded music at a Tennessee retreat built in 1998; after more than 65 gold and platinum albums were made there, the 10-acre studio estate is now listed for $19.5 million
articles.summary: A Tennessee retreat where Taylor Swift and Dolly Parton have recorded music is now on the market for $19.5 million.
articles.body: A Tennessee retreat where Taylor Swift and Dolly Parton have recorded music is now on the market for $19.5 million. Dark Horse Estate in Franklin, built in 1998 on just over 10 acres, has hosted more than 65 gold and platinum albums and is being offered as a rare combination of private residence, working studio, and entertainment compound, according to Realtor.com.The 23,138 square foot property includes Dark Horse Manor, Dark Horse Recording, The Cottage, The Bungalow Apartment, and The Party Barn. Its listing presents it as a place where artists can escape, focus, and create, with multiple studios, guest quarters, gathering spaces, and room for entertaining.A studio with a serious track recordDark Horse Recording has become one of the more notable creative spaces in the Nashville area. The estate has been used by artists including Taylor Swift, Dolly Parton, Keith Urban, Reba McEntire, Amy Grant, Peter Frampton, Florida Georgia Line, and Darius Rucker.More than 65 gold and platinum albums have been recorded there, according to the listing. That history gives the property a cultural identity that goes beyond its square footage or acreage.The studio is not just a feature of the home. It is a central part of the estate’s identity, making the listing appealing to buyers who want a live and work property with an established creative pedigree.What the estate containsDark Horse Manor is the main residence and offers facilities for recording music. The Cottage and The Bungalow Apartment offer private guest accommodations, allowing visiting artists or collaborators to stay on site.The Party Barn is another layer of appeal to the property. It gives the estate a place to hold gatherings, events or creative sessions beyond the studio itself. The compound also includes a three car garage, covered walkways, a sky bridge, and a game room. These details suggest that the property was designed not only for recording but for a lifestyle built around privacy, hospitality, and creative work, as per the report.Outdoor space built for inspirationThe estate sits on 10.01 acres, offering a level of privacy that is hard to find close to Nashville. The grounds are intended as a retreat, with natural surroundings and space to get away from the pace of the city.More than 3,000 square feet of covered porches and walkways overlook the property. These outdoor areas are intended for entertaining and relaxation, but they also give the estate a calm atmosphere that can support creative work.The combination of indoor studios and outdoor space makes the property more than a typical luxury listing. It is built for people who want to live, work, host guests, and create in one place.Why the price is $19.5 millionThe $19.5 million asking price reflects more than the size of the home. It reflects the land, the scale of the compound, the recording facilities, and the estate’s history with major artists.The property has already drawn attention, reaching the top of Realtor.com’s weekly most popular homes list. That visibility may help attract buyers who understand the value of a turnkey creative estate.For a buyer in the music industry, the estate offers an immediate opportunity to continue operating a studio with a proven track record. For a private buyer, it offers a rare chance to own a large, secluded property with built in entertainment and guest space.A property with a storyDark Horse Estate is not being marketed as just another luxury home. It is being sold as a piece of Nashville’s creative history, with a list of artists whose work has passed through its studios.The fact that Taylor Swift and Dolly Parton are among the names associated with the property gives it a level of recognition that most estates cannot match. That history may matter as much to buyers as the physical features of the home.As the listing moves forward, the question is whether the next owner will preserve the estate’s role as a working studio or reshape it into a private residence. Either way, the property enters the market with a story that few homes can claim.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: 'Heavens will not fall': SC on ED plea challenging Azam Khan's interim bail
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to stay the Allahabad high court order granting interim bail to Samajwadi Party leader Azam Khan in a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to stay the Allahabad high court order granting interim bail to Samajwadi Party leader Azam Khan in a money laundering case. The court observed that "heavens will not fall" if the order was allowed to stand.However, a bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant agreed to hear the Enforcement Directorate's appeal on Thursday.The ED had approached the Supreme Court challenging the high court's decision, arguing that the interim bail order was passed in haste and without giving the agency adequate opportunity to present its case.When the ED sought a status quo on the high court order, a bench comprising CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana refused to intervene immediately. "Let him be on interim bail. Heavens will not fall if we do not stay the HC order," the bench said.Appearing for the ED, Additional Solicitor General SV Raju submitted that the high court had effectively decided the matter finally through an interim order. He also argued that the agency was not allowed to file its complete counter-affidavit and that its request for a trial court report on the service of arrest papers to Khan was not considered.The CJI directed that the matter be listed for hearing on Thursday.The Allahabad High Court had granted interim bail to the 78-year-old SP leader on Tuesday in the money laundering case, observing that the ED had failed to furnish written grounds of arrest when taking him into custody on October 31.The high court had also described the proceedings as "motivated" and "mala fide", pointing out that Khan was arrested moments after being released from jail in another case. It had granted the ED a week to file its counter-affidavit.Khan, who is lodged at Dasna jail in Ghaziabad, was arrested in connection with a money laundering probe linked to the Maulana Mohammad Ali Jauhar Trust and the construction of the Mohammad Ali Jauhar University in Rampur.His interim bail came on a day when the Supreme Court also dismissed the Uttar Pradesh government's appeal against the suspension of his conviction in the fake birth certificate case, while granting similar relief to his wife, Tazeen Fatma, and son, Abdullah Azam Khan.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Hakeem Jeffries faces first test in bid to become first Black US House speaker
articles.summary: Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries faces a significant test on Wednesday as he moves closer to making history as the first black speaker of the US house of
articles.body: Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries faces a significant test on Wednesday as he moves closer to making history as the first black speaker of the US house of representatives. House democrats will hold a private meeting to elect their leadership for the upcoming Congress and nominate Jeffries for the top position.Despite running unopposed, Jeffries faces growing unease within his party, with several members and supporters demanding a change in leadership. The calls for a fresh approach have intensified following voters' decision to remove republicans from power in a setback for president Donald Trump and his party.Democrats have received a flood of phone calls and social media messages from constituents and newly elected lawmakers demanding a fresh start. According to AP, protesters also heckled Jeffries at a Democratic conference in Denver last week.Before Wednesday's closed-door election, Jeffries, a New York representative, said he was not taking support for granted. He has been holding discussions with the various House Democratic caucuses and reaching out to nearly every member of the incoming majority. He is also seeking a recorded vote to give lawmakers an opportunity to express their positions.“I embrace those conversations,” he said.Jeffries is part of a three-member leadership team that includes Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California. All three are contesting their respective positions without opposition. Their election would also mark historic milestones, with Clark becoming the first woman to serve as majority leader and Aguilar the first Latino majority whip.Jeffries will need to secure a separate vote in the full House when the new Congress begins on January 3, 2027, to officially become speaker.Questions emerge over Democratic leadershipWednesday's election will be the first major leadership vote for dozens of newly elected lawmakers, even before they formally take their seats in January. However, the democrats' sizeable incoming majority is expected to give Jeffries a comfortable advantage.Rep.-elect Brad Lander of New York declared his support for Jeffries, when he launched his congressional campaign. Meanwhile, Rep.-elect Randy Villegas of California said he would back whoever could help him deliver the best results for his Central Valley constituency.Returning Rep. Emily Randall, D-Wash., said questions about the party's house leadership had surfaced during town hall meetings in her constituency. She has also received numerous instagram direct messages from people seeking answers about the leadership contest, prompting her to contact some of them directly.“People have messaged me asking if Bernie Sanders could be the speaker of the house,” Randall said. “Technically yes, and it would be probably difficult.”Although the house has the authority to elect anyone as its speaker, Sanders is an unlikely choice because he currently serves in the US senate.Recalling one conversation with a constituent, Randall said she heard his concerns before explaining why she believed Jeffries was the right candidate.“Truthfully, not like blowing smoke, whoever is our speaker — and I think it is going to be Hakeem Jeffries, and I am supporting Hakeem Jeffries for speaker — I think we will accomplish a lot of the things that he was asking us to,” she said.Several lawmakers also referred to a livestream by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, in which she attempted to explain the responsibilities of the house speaker and address questions surrounding the leadership race.“There is one candidate in this race: Hakeem Jeffries,” Ocasio-Cortez said at the Capitol. “I think that everyone is far more concerned what that leadership means, what is it promising.”New leadership marks post-Pelosi transitionJeffries, Clark and Aguilar have advanced through the democratic ranks together, emerging as the first new generation of leaders following Nancy Pelosi's departure from the party's top leadership positions. Their upcoming tenure will also mark their first experience leading house democrats from the majority.Pelosi's decision to relinquish her leadership position in 2022, following the Democrats' electoral defeat that handed control of the House to Republicans, paved the way for the transition. Pelosi, former Democratic leader Steny Hoyer of Maryland and Rep. James Clyburn of South Carolina had worked closely together throughout their leadership careers before stepping away from their long-held positions.A similar leadership contest is unfolding in the senate, where democratic leader Chuck Schumer faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland as members push for a change in direction.However, returning Rep.Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz, said the leadership situations in the house and senate “are quite different”.Ansari described Jeffries as an inclusive and collaborative leader who listens to suggestions from progressive lawmakers, including members of the progressive caucus. She said his responsibility was to represent the entire democratic party rather than cater to a particular group.“His job is to reflect all of us, not just a faction,” Ansari said.She added that democrats would benefit more from concentrating on their legislative priorities and preparations for governing than getting caught up in leadership disagreements.“It is more productive to focus on preparing on what we're going to do in the majority, and what we need and want to get done in those first 100 days,” she said.Rep. Shomari Figures of Alabama, who secured an unexpected victory in a redrawn congressional district that favoured Republicans, also confirmed his support for Jeffries.Figures said backing Jeffries was an easy decision, crediting him with steering the party through an exceptionally turbulent two-year period.He said Jeffries “led us through what is likely the most tumultuous two-year tenure of any presidency in the history of this nation.”“I’m not going to not stand by him right here on the precipice of history,” Figures said.You use AI every day. articles.title: During World War II, A. Paroli mailed a coconut to F. Rochetti in Santa Rosa; its shell carried the address, and naval mail routed it through San Francisco
articles.summary: Discover the fascinating story of A. Paroli's coconut mail sent to F. Rochetti during World War II, showcasing innovative military correspondence and its journey through Navy mail to Santa Rosa, California.
articles.body: In World War II, the overseas-based military men used various approaches for staying in touch with their family at home. While some preferred to send letters or postcards, others mailed personal items. A. Paroli, a member of Construction Battalion Maintenance Unit 511, sent F. Rochetti in Santa Rosa, California, a coconut.Rather than putting it in a box or covering it with traditional wrapping paper, he used the shell of this fruit to write the address of the recipient along with his military address. The coconut traveled through Navy mail and eventually arrived in California. This unique item of wartime correspondence can be seen in the collection of the Museum of Sonoma County. The Museum of Sonoma County posted the story on its Collections Spotlight blog in 2020. Eric Stanley, the museum’s associate director and curator of history, wrote the post.The coconut carried its own mailing addressOn the face of the coconut was written: “To F. Rochetti, Phillips Ave., Santa Rosa, Calif.” On the backside of the coconut was written “From A. Paroli, C.B.M.U. 511-% F.P.O. San Francisco, CA.” Instead of a normal package, Paroli utilised the coconut’s exterior shell to write the postal address. The Museum of Sonoma County calls it one of the most unusual examples of military correspondence in its collection. This postal address also gave information about how this must have been mailed. According to the museum, it was transported by Navy ship to the F.P.O. in San Francisco, from where it reached the Santa Rosa post office and was delivered to Rochetti.Its exact origin remains unknownParoli was a member of Construction Battalion Maintenance Unit 511, which operated on the islands of Efate and Tongatapu in 1943 and 1944, respectively, according to the museum. Both islands had coconuts, but nothing in the museum’s records says which island Paroli found this one on. The coconut was sent from an unspecified location.There is also no information in the museum about the exact date on which the coconut was mailed. Therefore, the location and date of the mailing are unknown. The return address is the only information about its mailing route, which is the San Francisco Fleet Post Office, where the mail was processed before reaching California.A small piece of wartime history preserved in CaliforniaThe coconut became part of the Museum of Sonoma County’s collection. The unique shape of the coconut sets it apart from the letters and traditional packages used for wartime communication. In the same section of the museum, one can see yet another example of the unusual mailing of the item related to the region. It is the seed catalogue, which was sent internationally by the horticulturist Luther Burbank in 1920. Paroli’s coconut preserves the handwritten address, the sender and recipient names, the military unit and the postal route. Though the point from which the mailing took place is not clear, the object is the documentation of how one of the servicemen sent the unusual package from the Pacific to Santa Rosa during World War II. All these artifacts help us understand that this service was not only an act of delivering something but also a way of bringing together distant places, families and communities. Through letters of wartime, through foreign horticulture catalogs, people were able to preserve their stories, connect the town with the rest of the world and document ordinary things.You use AI every day. articles.title: British hacker who stole $11m jailed for six years in US
articles.summary: Tyler Buchanan, from Dundee, was a member of the notorious Scattered Spider group and began hacking when he was a teenager.
articles.body:
A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message phishing, and stealing more than $11.6m (£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims.

Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, started hacking as a teenager and was part of the collective of young hackers known as Scattered Spider, which has been blamed for a string of high profile cyber-crimes.

US prosecutors said the thefts had "severe, life-altering consequences" for victims and showed the growing threat posed by online crime groups.

The sentence brings to an end a years-long international investigation involving authorities in the UK, US, Spain and Canada.

Buchanan admitted taking part in a hacking campaign that began in 2021, when he was 19.

Working from his parents' home, he and other English-speaking hackers in the US and UK targeted employees at major technology and telecommunications companies.

It made them $8m in less than two years, according to US prosecutors.

Buchanan and his hacker gang sent out hundreds of SMS messages to the mobile phones of people who worked for large tech or telecoms companies.

The SMS phishing messages contained links to spoof websites designed to look like legitimate sites of victim companies.

The group used messages like "Hi, your account is due to expire - you need to log in to your work account here immediately or you will lose access to work apps".

The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), and account usernames and passwords.

The boys and young men did it on an industrial scale with Buchanan setting up a Telegram bot to collect all the victims' credentials as the duped workers unwittingly handed over their login details.

For some victim companies, subsequently stolen information included confidential work information, intellectual property, plus account access credentials, names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.

The group then used stolen information and SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors in the United States.

In the largest single theft, prosecutors said one victim lost $1.67m in December 2022.

Overall, authorities calculated that Buchanan and his co-conspirators stole more than $11.6m from victims.

Buchanan was also a victim of cyber-criminals.

In early 2023 his online identity and home address were leaked by rival hackers seeking access to his cryptocurrency.

Cyber security researchers and journalists reported that he was assaulted at his home and threatened with a blowtorch.

"TylerB and his group were highly sophisticated and organised but the violence he and others experienced was a sign of the troubling direction of these online communities of young hackers" says cyber security researcher Allison Nixon from Unit221B.

Buchanan then reportedly fled to Canada to escape further threats before returning home.

In April 2023, officers from Police Scotland searched Buchanan's bedroom after receiving a request from the FBI.

Investigators recovered a device containing the names and addresses of hacking victims, along with cryptocurrency seed phrases and account credentials belonging to at least one victim.

The following month, Buchanan left the UK again.

He was arrested on 31 May 2024 at Palma de Mallorca Airport in Spain while attempting to board a private flight to Naples.

After being extradited to the United States, he remained in custody before being sentenced this week.

In his November 2023 charge, Buchanan was named along with four American men and boys in their twenties and teens for alleged activity linked to the notorious cyber-criminal collective Scattered Spider.

They have all pleaded guilty too and are now serving time in jail.

Two other members of the Scattered Spider group were jailed in the UK in July for various cyber attacks including a disruptive one against Transport for London that caused £39m of damage.

articles.title: Meghan Markle’s father faces new child sex abuse complaints in the Philippines
articles.summary: Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was charged with the possession of child abuse material, police in the Philippines said.
articles.body: Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, has had criminal complaints filed against him over alleged online child sexual abuse offences, police in the Philippines said Wednesday. The complaints accuse Markle of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation of children, police told Reuters. They added that the complaints were filed before the prosecutor’s office in Cebu on Monday, following an investigation last month into the alleged distribution and possession of child sexual abuse materials. Markle had lived in Cebu for a period before returning to the United States. Prosecutors the evaluating the charges filed by police before they decide whether to issue a subpoena against Markle whose legal team would have 10 days to respond with a counter-affidavit. Prosecutors would then decide whether to proceed with a court case. Prince Harry and Meghan’s spokesperson declined to comment when NBC News asked about the latest charges. The announcement came less than two weeks after the 82-year-old was arrested in Florida and charged with one count of possession of child pornography, according to a criminal complaint filed by the Justice Department. The FBI seized around 78 items from two storage units rented by Markle in Los Angeles, that contained “suspected child pornography,” according to court documents. Items seized include film negatives featuring an adult man with naked “pre-pubescent” girls, the complaint said, which added that a witness “positively identified the adult man as Markle.” Based on background in one photo, the FBI determined the images found in California were taken in a hotel in the Philippines, according to the court document. Markle was taken into custody in Tampa, Florida, and was later released under house arrest. But after he cut off his ankle monitor, a federal judge ordered last week that Markle remain in custody for violating the conditions of his release. Markle had been living in a senior care facility in Lakeland, Florida after he was forced to return to the U.S. from the Philippines when he suffered a stroke and a leg was amputated, according to The Associated Press. The retired television lighting and photography director denied the allegations last month, calling them “sick lies.” Meghan Markle asaid in a statement last month that she was “deeply distressed” by the allegations against her father. Their relationship has been limited and fraught in recent years, with her father not attending her wedding to Harry in 2018 amid widespread media scrutiny. Her statement said that she was previously informed of “disturbing allegations” against him, with British police subsequently confirming she was passed a letter in January 2019 “containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.” London’s Metropolitan Police said it had not informed other law enforcement agencies about the allegations in the letter at the time, referring itself to Britain’s policing watchdog over the handling of the allegations. “The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” said Meghan, who said she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.” Meghan Markle and her husband, Prince Harry, stepped back as working royals in 2020 amid widespread reports of a royal rift and moved to, leaving Britain for California. Harry, the second son of King Charles III and the late Princess Diana, leveled harsh criticism at Buckingham Palace and other senior royals across a series of media interviews and a tell-all memoir, “Spare.” The couple returned to Britain two months ago, with their two children moving to schools in the country.

articles.title: Chapelcross data centre plans generate biggest response ever
articles.summary: Dumfries and Galloway Council has received more than 10,000 representations about the Chapelcross plans.
articles.body:
A data centre at a former nuclear site in southern Scotland has generated the most representations ever received by a council's planning department.

The local authority in Dumfries and Galloway is working its way through more than 10,000 submissions over CX Tech's proposals for the Chapelcross site near Annan.

A final consultation window closes on 29 November and, once it passes, planning officers will complete the processing and verification of the representations received.

The council said the total number of representations, names of those making them and a summary of matters raised would be made available on its website "well ahead" of any decision on the plan's fate.

"We appreciate the significant public interest in this application and thank members of the public for their patience while this work is undertaken," it added.

Outlander star criticises data centre plan for nuclear site

Giant data centre plans lodged for old nuclear plant site

The nuclear plant stopped electricity production more than 20 years ago.

Plans were lodged seeking planning permission in principle in September for the £16.5bn data centre.

Developers said it could support up to 750 jobs during construction and about 540 once operational, plus hundreds of indirect posts.

They described it as a "once-in-a-generation opportunity for Dumfries and Galloway and for Scotland".

However, a campaign was launched against the project almost as soon as it emerged with fears being raised about the impact on household bills and the strain on the energy grid.

It has also questioned the job creation claims as well as saying the "large scale industrialisation" of the area was unacceptable.

Thousands of people joined a protest in Edinburgh at the weekend against the building of large-scale AI data centres.

New Scottish government planning guidance is due to be published soon.

Kim Cairns, a campaigner against the Chapelcross project, said the scheme - which would be one of the largest in the world - would be a "monstrosity on the environment".

The council has already said that due to the number of representations received, it would not be able to publish them all online as it usually would.

Instead, it said the number of representations received in support and objection to the application would be recorded and published online along with a summary of the "material grounds for commenting".

articles.title: The FBI is changing how it fights crime and protects Americans in their communities
articles.summary: Under President Donald Trump, the FBI says it made 71,650 violent crime arrests in 21 months, up 114%, and seized enough fentanyl to kill 350 million.
articles.body: When President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, America faced one of the highest threat environments in its history. Years of open borders, soft-on-crime policies and a government that turned its back on law enforcement had left our communities vulnerable and our law enforcement officers without the support they deserved. Under Trump’s leadership, we set out to reverse that tide. We rebuilt the FBI around its core mission: protecting the American people. We changed our priorities, revitalized partnerships, overhauled our technology and transformed the Bureau into a more aggressive, effective crime-fighting organization. The results: Over the last 21 months, this FBI made 71,650 violent crime arrests, a 114% increase compared to the final 21 months of the previous administration. We seized 4,616 kilograms of deadly drugs, up 32%, including enough fentanyl to potentially kill more than 350 million Americans. FBI REPORTS 114% JUMP IN VIOLENT CRIME ARRESTS UNDER TRUMP COMPARED TO BIDEN’S FINAL MONTHS We identified or located 5,801 child victims, up 25%, many of whom were trafficked, exploited or abused. We made 6,744 arrests tied to foreign terrorist organizations, an increase of 1,057%, and disrupted more than 1,300 terrorists. We arrested 10 fugitives from the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, including alleged murderers, rapists and other violent criminals. That is 2.5 times the number arrested during the previous four years combined. And through the historic, first-ever Most Wanted Fraudsters list, led by Vice President JD Vance and the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, we arrested six alleged fraudsters in three-and-a-half months who were collectively responsible for $2.1 billion in alleged fraud. WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD These results were no accident. They were the product of deliberate decisions to change how the FBI operates, where we deploy our resources and how we work with our law enforcement partners. First, we put violent crime back at the center of the FBI’s mission On my first day as director, we made crushing violent crime a top priority. Previously, it barely ranked among the Bureau’s top 10 priorities. We changed that immediately. Today, "Crush Violent Crime" is more than a slogan. It drives our operations, our resource decisions and our commitment to the American people. FBI TOUTS 6,000 ARRESTS, 44% HOMICIDE DROP ONE YEAR INTO TRUMP'S DC CRIME CRACKDOWN We then put our people where they could make the greatest impact. This FBI moved nearly 2,000 personnel out of Washington and back into the field. Agents, analysts and FBI teams solve cases in the field, in neighborhoods and alongside local officers who know their communities, not from conference rooms at headquarters. We shifted our focus away from Pennsylvania Avenue and back to Main Street America. Second, we rebuilt and strengthened our law enforcement partnerships The FBI cannot succeed alone. Our greatest strength comes from working shoulder to shoulder with the men and women of state, local, tribal and federal law enforcement. FBI ANNOUNCES 305 ARRESTS, 24 MISSING CHILDREN RECOVERED IN CHICAGO DURING OPERATION NEW DAWN Through our 59 Homeland Security Task Forces, 200 Joint Terrorism Task Forces, 30 Safe Trails Task Forces and other partnerships, we have strengthened coordination across agencies and delivered major joint operations. Operation Summer Heat, our three-month violent crime surge, brought law enforcement together to target dangerous criminals nationwide with more than 9,000 violent crime arrests, a 3% increase from the record number of arrests in summer 2025. Operation Steadfast Promise deployed 500 FBI personnel to combat violent crime on tribal lands, representing the largest commitment to Indian Country in Bureau history — with surges like Operation Not Forgotten, where this FBI executed 118 arrests with Indian Country partners — up 123% from last year’s operation and bringing us to over 1,000 Indian Country arrests in 2026. KASH PATEL TOUTS FBI 'FULL-THROTTLE MISSION' AFTER OPERATION SPRING CLEANING YIELDS 615 INDICTMENTS/COMPLAINTS We added 2,770 Task Force Officers across the country by eliminating wasteful administrative bureaucracy that saw a 14-month onboarding process shrink to less than 30 days, allowing our agents to partner directly alongside state, local, tribal or other federal law enforcement officers. We then put our people where they could make the greatest impact. This FBI moved nearly 2,000 personnel out of Washington and back into the field. We also expanded our capabilities to confront emerging threats. Through our first-of-its-kind counter-unmanned aircraft systems (counter-UAS) school at the FBI’s Redstone Arsenal, we equipped local law enforcement partners to detect, track and respond to dangerous drones. During the 2026 FIFA World Cup, those efforts helped lead to the seizure of more than 700 drones. EXCLUSIVE: FBI EXTRADITIONS SOAR AS PATEL RAMPS UP FOREIGN OUTREACH, VOWS 'NO SANCTUARY' And our reach extends beyond America's borders. We increased foreign transfers of custody to 84, up 71%, and extraditions to 157, up 121%. These are dangerous fugitives and alleged criminals who can no longer evade American justice simply by crossing an international border. Third, we modernized the FBI to meet today's threats FBI OVERHAULS TECH BACKBONE TO COUNTER AI THREATS FROM FOREIGN ADVERSARIES, REDUCE RESPONSE TIMES, PATEL SAYS For too long, outdated technology and bureaucratic processes slowed the Bureau's ability to deliver results. We changed that. The FBI increased its use of superintelligence by 605% compared to 2024, putting this FBI on a course to save nearly 640,000 labor hours, the equivalent of about 79,000 workdays, by synthesizing data and streamlining administrative paperwork. In less than two years, our Laboratory Division eliminated a four-year DNA backlog involving 1.8 million samples. We transformed our headquarters’ operational command and control center, standing up the first-ever "Director’s Strategic Information Group" — cutting DNA processing and producing finalized reporting in just 20 minutes, compared to what took hours in the old system. We also achieved compliance with mandatory insider threat requirements for the first time since the policy took effect in 2021. And through Operation Blackout, our campaign against transnational scam centers, we are dismantling sophisticated criminal networks that prey on Americans. Our efforts have resulted in shuttering dozens of scam compounds overseas, more than $17 billion in seizures and prevented over 11,000 Americans from being scammed out of nearly $700 million in cyber-enabled fraud schemes. articles.title: A West Virginia woman lost data when a replacement laptop failed; after the company missed her lawsuit for 18 months, the state's top court left $15,507.92 in compensatory damages intact
articles.summary: For any consumer who has ever watched a hard drive crash without a backup, losing years of personal files is a familiar nightmare, yet few expect that
articles.body: For any consumer who has ever watched a hard drive crash without a backup, losing years of personal files is a familiar nightmare, yet few expect that frustration to end in a multi-year legal battle reaching the highest court in the state. In a ruling issued by the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia, technology giant HP Inc. failed in its bid to overturn a $15,507.92 compensatory damages award granted to a customer after both her original laptop and a warranty replacement broke down, erasing her stored data.A costly default after eighteen months of silenceThe dispute dates back to July 2019, when West Virginia resident Ms. Thomas purchased an HP laptop at a Best Buy retail store for $1,527.98 and later added a three-year extended warranty, according to records reviewed by the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia. When technical problems plagued the original computer and technicians could not fix it, HP provided a replacement machine under the warranty agreement. However, that replacement unit also failed roughly six months later, wiping out Ms. Thomas’s stored data and leaving repair technicians unable to restore it.Frustrated by the repeated hardware failures and seeking a purchase-price refund alongside compensation for unauthorized and excessive Instant Ink subscription charges, Ms. Thomas filed a civil lawsuit. HP never responded to the complaint for approximately eighteen months, an oversight the company later attributed to an internal misrouting of legal paperwork to an employee on medical leave, the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia noted. In November 2022, a circuit court entered an amended default judgment awarding Ms. Thomas $15,507.92 in compensatory damages, covering the defective laptop, a replacement device, ink charges, and inconvenience, alongside $20,000 in punitive damages and $9,130.33 in legal costs and attorney fees.High Court upholds compensatory awardOnce HP discovered the judgment and sought to set it aside under state procedural rules, the company argued that the lower court lacked jurisdiction because the initial complaint did not meet the financial threshold and contended that internal administrative error constituted excusable neglect. Both the circuit court and the Intermediate Court of Appeals rejected HP’s effort to erase the default judgment, prompting the company to appeal to the state’s highest bench.The Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia affirmed the decision to leave the default judgment and the $15,507.92 compensatory award intact. Reading the consumer’s initial complaint favorably, the justices concluded that Ms. Thomas had sufficiently alleged $10,000 in damages to establish the circuit court’s jurisdiction. Furthermore, the court determined that misrouting a lawsuit to an absent employee did not excuse an eighteen-month failure to appear in court, meaning HP failed to demonstrate the good cause required to reopen the underlying liability ruling.Scrutiny over punitive damagesWhile the compensatory award survived intact, the litigation surrounding the $20,000 punitive damages component drew sharp scrutiny during appellate review. Under West Virginia civil procedure rules governing default judgments, a court generally cannot grant relief that differs in kind or exceeds the specific amount requested in a plaintiff’s original complaint. Although the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia found that HP had waived certain appellate arguments regarding the punitive award by failing to brief them properly, the case sparked a notable dissent from the bench. One justice dissenting noted that Ms. Thomas never sought punitive damages or alleged facts warranting them in her initial filing. Any punitive damages beyond $10,000 in the complaint would violate procedural safeguards, the justice said. The majority's memorandum decision holds HP liable for compensatory damages and attorney fees from its prolonged courtroom absence.Image Courtesy: Google GeminiYou use AI every day. articles.title: Prince William takes in Bollywood as Kate visits Mumbai hospital on royal tour of India
articles.summary: Britain’s Prince William watched Bollywood dances and toured a film studio in Mumbai on the last day of his royal visit to India on Wednesday, while his wife, Kate, spoke to health workers at a maternity hospital in the city.
articles.body: Britain’s Prince William watched Bollywood dances and toured a film studio in Mumbai on the last day of his royal visit to India on Wednesday, while his wife, Kate, spoke to health workers at a maternity hospital in the city. The royal couple, who are on a three-day visit to India’s financial capital, will end their trip in New Delhi and meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi late on Wednesday. William and Kate had separate engagements on Wednesday, with the prince visiting the office of a prominent Bollywood production house, Dharma Productions, in suburban Mumbai, while Kate visited a maternity hospital in the center of the city. William smiled and clapped as dancers moved to a number from Dharma’s hit Bollywood movie, “Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham” (Joy Sometimes, Sorrow Sometimes), which is set partly in London. Actors Saif Ali Khan and Kareena Kapoor were also present. “He was gracious and kind and spoke extensively about the potential of Indian cinema and how cinema across all Indian languages is loved worldwide,” said filmmaker Karan Johar, who runs Dharma Productions, after the visit. The royal couple have been on a whirlwind tour of the city of 13 million since Monday, playing cricket with the retired Sachin Tendulkar, visiting a craft school and attending the glittering award ceremony for the Earthshot Prize, a climate-change award that William set up six years ago. The Princess of Wales, on her most high-profile overseas visit since receiving treatment for cancer in 2024, also presented one of the awards on Tuesday night, wearing a bright red Indian-style gown. In his speech at the awards ceremony on Tuesday, William said the impact of global warming was becoming conspicuous, with repeated heatwaves and devastating floods, calling it a pivotal moment for the planet.

articles.title: EasyJet flight makes emergency landing at Bristol Airport
articles.summary: The flight, bound for Edinburgh, is forced to return to Bristol Airport shortly after take off.
articles.body:
A passenger plane was forced to make an emergency landing after it was struck by a bird.

Flight EZY213 departed Bristol Airport for Edinburgh at approximately 09:24 GMT, but returned to the airport shortly after 10:00 due to suffering a bird strike during take-off.

A spokesperson for EasyJet said nobody was hurt in the incident and the plane landed back in Bristol safely, adding the aircraft was met by the emergency services as a precaution in line with standard procedures.

The spokesperson also said: "While this was outside of our control, we would like to apologise for the inconvenience caused and we have arranged for a replacement aircraft to continue the flight to Edinburgh this morning."

articles.title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Tyler Robinson defense wants testing on bullet fragments paused in assassination of Charlie Kirk
articles.summary: Tyler Robinson's lawyers want Utah ballistics testing paused as prosecutors push FBI virtual comparison microscopy on Charlie Kirk's autopsy fragments.
articles.body: Attorneys for Charlie Kirk's accused assassin Tyler Robinson are asking a Utah judge to put additional ballistics testing on pause as prosecutors attempt to conclusively link bullet fragments recovered at autopsy to the suspected murder weapon, which some experts call unnecessary and even prosecutors admit isn't central to their case. The Utah County Attorney's Office has asked the judge to deny the motion, countering that the testing they are seeking will not consume the evidence or prevent Robinson's experts from having a look at it once the government is done — and that they have more compelling evidence to introduce at trial. "There is no reason to believe the bullet fragments contain exculpatory evidence," Deputy Utah County Attorney Ryan McBride alleged in an opposition to the defense motion. "To the contrary, all the evidence points to the inculpatory value of the fragments." TYLER ROBINSON JUDGE UNSEALS ATF REPORT IN ASSASSINATION OF CHARLIE KIRK Robinson has allegedly admitted to the shooting, he wrote. Three unspent cartridges in the rifle were consistent with the gunshot fired at Kirk. The bullet fragments were consistent with the suspected murder weapon, although they have not been conclusively identified to it. And police recovered video evidence and a Dremel tool consistent with etchings made on brass casings recovered in the rifle at the scene. While the fragment testing, known as virtual comparison microscopy (VCM), won't destroy the evidence, it is expected to physically alter or even damage it, according to court filings. "Petals" from the fragments may be folded out of the way as investigators look for rifling markings on the underlying surface, according to prosecutors. The fragments may be cleaned, at least in a small area. And lead fragments may be cleaned or scraped. There is a risk that pieces break off during the process. TYLER ROBINSON'S DEFENSE TEAM FIGHTS TO SEAL EVIDENCE AND PUNISH PROSECUTORS IN CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION Robinson's lawyers want the VCM testing placed on hold until they have a chance to examine and photograph the same evidence — or an order allowing a defense expert to observe the testing in person or via a video recording, something the FBI does not allow for a number of reasons, including contamination and national security concerns. They argued that prior ATF testing already damaged the evidence, and the next round of testing could result in further harm. CHARLIE KIRK JUDGE DENIES TYLER ROBINSON'S ATTEMPT TO HAVE POTENTIAL DEATH PENALTY REMOVED "The ATF couldn’t conclusively connect the bullet fragment to the recovered rifle, but it couldn’t rule out the rifle either," said Jason Pack, a retired FBI supervisory agent who has been following the case. "That’s an important distinction, and it helps explain why prosecutors want the FBI to take another look." He explained that VCM is a more advanced process than simply looking at the fragments under a microscope, a more traditional method. Even so, there's no guarantee that examiners will find a more conclusive link between the fragments and the suspected murder weapon. CHARLIE KIRK'S FAMILY COMES FACE TO FACE WITH ACCUSED ASSASSIN FOR FIRST TIME "If the markings are too damaged or simply aren’t there anymore, even the best technology can’t bring them back," Pack told Fox News Digital. Robinson is accused of shooting Kirk at Utah Valley University during a Turning Point USA public speaking event on Sept. 10, 2025. During Kirk's autopsy, investigators recovered a bullet jacket fragment and four lead fragments from his body, according to prosecutors. CHARLIE KIRK MURDER CASE AS 'STRAIGHT-FORWARD' AS IT GETS, PROSECUTORS ARGUE AS CASE NEARS TRIAL DECISION "If the bullet fragment is again altered to the point where no independent comparison is possible, then the degree of prejudice to the defendant is severe," Robinson's lawyers wrote to the court. "The defense will be unable to independently verify conclusions, cross-examination will be unfairly limited, and the jury will hear unchallengeable expert testimony." Bernard Zapor, a former ATF special agent in charge and faculty associate at Arizona State University, said those concerns may be overblown. The fragments were already documented meticulously during the ATF's initial examination, he said, with photographs, data and images available to the defense through discovery. If the fragments are damaged during additional testing, it may not change much, since the initial testing was inconclusive — which he said is not unusual in shootings involving similar caliber weapons. TYLER ROBINSON HEARING ENDS WITHOUT RULING AS EVIDENCE DISMANTLES CHARLIE KIRK CONSPIRACY CLAIMS "This is all distracting from the purpose of getting information to the jury so they can come to a conclusion, one way or the other," he told Fox News Digital. "This case is solid. You don’t want to do anything to disrupt it." Robinson's lawyers previously flagged in court that they intend to challenge the ATF's findings and methodology. During prior testing, ATF examiner Samantha Karner cleaned the jacket fragment, photographed it and then peeled the "petals" back to examine groove impressions on it. She identified the fragment as having been in the .30 caliber class, but she was unable to conclusively link it to the suspected murder weapon, Robinson's grandfather's .30-06 Mauser rifle. TYLER ROBINSON'S AND LANCE TWIGGS' DNA BOTH ALLEGEDLY FOUND ON KEY EVIDENCE IN CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION "Given the limited detail that Ms. Karner observed, she could not include or exclude the fragment as having been fired from the recovered rifle," prosecutors wrote. "She testified that there was 'no further testing that [she] could do' to try to reach a conclusive result ... However, she noted 'the possibility of using a 3D system to visualize the individual characteristics on the bullet,' to obtain more conclusive results." For that kind of analysis, however, the fragments would need to be sent to the FBI for VCM. TYLER ROBINSON TO FACE TRIAL IN CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION AS JUDGE KEEPS DEATH PENALTY ON TABLE "This analysis is non-destructive and uses 3D technology to capture multiple scans of the object," prosecutors wrote. "The scan data will be preserved and provided to the defense for their own analysis." SEND US A TIP In order to perform the scans, however, analysts may have to clean the fragments or fold back warped metal, called "petals," to expose the surface of the fragment that contacted the rifle when fired, prosecutors wrote. TYLER ROBINSON PROSECUTORS: NO DNA, NO PROBLEM — PILE OF EVIDENCE TO PUSH CHARLIE KIRK CASE TOWARD JUSTICE Prosecutors are also seeking another type of testing, known as metallurgical testing, on the bullet jacket fragment and at least one piece of lead, according to court filings. That testing might require cleaning "around a small area," prosecutors added, before it is examined with an X-ray. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST "The FBI is also proposing separate testing to compare the metal in the recovered bullet fragments with ammunition seized during the investigation," Pack said. "That could provide additional information, although it wouldn’t conclusively identify the firearm." GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL Lastly, prosecutors want an examiner to disassemble one of the unfired .30-06 cartridges found at Robinson's home after his arrest, for comparison. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Robinson's attorneys entered not guilty pleas on his behalf to all charges. He could face the potential death penalty if convicted of the top count of aggravated murder.

articles.title: A Pennsylvania woman says her supplemental cancer insurance was cancelled after her breast cancer diagnosis; the insurer cites incorrect medical information on her application as the reason for denying her claim
articles.summary: Just like millions of people across the world, Jeanette Mozuch bought a supplemental cancer policy from Heartland National Life Insurance to protect
articles.body: Just like millions of people across the world, Jeanette Mozuch bought a supplemental cancer policy from Heartland National Life Insurance to protect herself if she ever got sick. After being diagnosed with breast cancer in February, she filed a claim. She thought her medical bills would be covered, but instead, she was told the company had dropped her coverage, according to a report by CBS.A health policy that didn’t helpMozuch, who lives in the Pittsburgh area, was diagnosed with breast cancer in February. She had recently got Medicare and wanted extra coverage. This was before the diagnosis. An insurance broker visited her home and offered her and her husband a policy from Heartland National Life Insurance. The plan pays cash benefits after certain diagnoses, including cancer, heart attack and stroke.The cost, she said, was $35 for the two of them, paid monthly. “You never know,” she told the broadcaster. “I thought it was worth getting it.” So they purchased it, thinking the insurance would help them on a dull day.A claim that was deniedThe health coverage started last autumn. In February, Mozuch’s doctor told her she had breast cancer. She would need surgery and radiotherapy. When she filed a claim, she received letters from the insurer asking for more time to review it. Later, the company dropped her coverage altogether. Why? Mozuch was told she had answered a question incorrectly on her application. The insurer pointed to “question 2A”. When KDKA reviewed the application, it could not find a question with that label.When she kept asking questions about the claim refusal, the company pointed to a question about medical advice. It asks whether, in the previous two years, a medical professional recommended cancer-related testing or monitoring, including mammograms, that the applicant did not complete. The insurer said her answer to that question was wrong.Mammograms were ordered for Mozuch in May and August 2024, and again in April 2025, the insurer claimed, pointing to the records. The company said those records do not show she completed them.Mozuch said she believes she applied for the insurance around August 2025. She was surprised to learn that mammograms had been ordered earlier, as she thought her next screening was due two years after her May 2023 mammogram.Federal guidelines generally recommend screening every two years for women between 40 and 74 who are at average risk. Those guidelines do not explain why additional mammograms were ordered or whether Mozuch was told about them. She had another mammogram in February 2026.The woman is planning to appeal the insurance denial. She also plans to work with her doctor to confirm the dates of her last three mammograms. But Mozuch feels this issue is larger than her case. “They’re taking people’s money,” she said.She wonders if the insurer has denied similar claims from other policyholders. “I don’t think it’s right. They denied me my money, and I have all the proof I had it, so if they did it to me, how many other people have they done it to?”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Daera failing to protect wild birds, OEP finds
articles.summary: The Office for Environmental Protection said Daera had not complied with environmental law requiring it to classify and update Special Protection Areas.
articles.body:
An investigation has found the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs is failing to protect wild birds.

The Office for Environmental Protection said Daera had not complied with environmental law requiring it to classify and update Special Protection Areas (SPAs).

Environment Minister Andrew Muir said their findings made for "uncomfortable reading".

SPAs are home to rare and threatened birds like the curlew and whooper swan, which continue to decline in Northern Ireland.

The OEP said action had not been taken to maintain or restore wild bird populations and their habitats.

The director of RSPB NI, Joanne Sherwood, said the findings were "no surprise" and called for urgent action.

The ongoing investigation began in 2024.

A parallel investigation is looking at the same issues involving Defra and Natural England, and they have also been issued with decision notices.

In Northern Ireland, the OEP's Chief Regulatory Officer Helen Venn acknowledged that "positive steps" had been taken, but added that delays in meeting legal obligations had played a part in the significant decline of wild birds in Northern Ireland.

"SPAs are important for achieving the Executive's commitments in relation to nature, such as the strategic outcome of thriving, resilient and connected nature and wildlife in the Environmental Improvement Plan.

"This is in addition to the Executive's international commitment to protect at least 30% of land and seas for nature's recovery by 2030.

"This is why it is important for Daera to carry out its legal responsibilities in a reasonable timeframe to deliver nature recovery and in relation to the classification and adaptation of SPAs on land."

The agriculture and environment minister Andrew Muir said there was "a moral and legal obligation" to protect wild bird habitats and welcomed continuing engagement between his officials and the OEP.

"The OEP has recognised in their investigation longstanding and concerning failures to implement recommended actions to protect wild bird habitats and populations by successive administrations both in England and Northern Ireland.

"While we have a long way to go to reverse current trends, there are signs of hope and clear examples of nature recovery in action.

"However, the scale of challenge requires greater levels of support from across government to provide the necessary resources and funding to address the nature crisis."

And he said the recently-published Nature Recovery Strategy and the Farming With Nature support package "reinforces" the department's commitment to nature restoration.

Sherwood said the group had been highlighting failing for decades.

"Today's findings from the OEP confirm what conservation organisations have been saying: action has been delayed for far too long.

"The focus must now move to delivery, with the Executive leading the way, and Daera and NIEA being resourced to take urgent action to put these protections in place and help reverse the decline of our most vulnerable bird populations.

"We hope today's OEP report will be the catalyst needed."

The decision notice is the latest step in the OEP's investigation.

It identifies failures and recommends what actions Daera should now take to fix them.

It says Daera has failed to classify and update SPAs, has not put measures in place to protect declining birds, and has not carried out a required review of habitats.

Recommendations include addressing outstanding recommendations "where they remain ecologically relevant" from a review of SPAs, carried out in Northern Ireland in 2001.

Where they cannot be implemented, it says "transparent, ornithological reasons" must be published.

Daera is also advised to identify the causes of declines and put in place resourced plans and effective measures to maintain or restore wild bird populations and the habitats they depend on.

And it says "the overdue habitat sufficiency review" must be carried out "as soon as practicably possible", to identify gaps in habitat provision and the action needed to address them.

articles.title: Rwanda and DRC: What is holding up the Washington peace process?
articles.summary: The two sides remain divided over key security commitments under the Washington Accords.
articles.body:
Another round of talks between the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Rwanda is reportedly expected to take place in Geneva on November 19 , as disagreements persist over implementing the Washington Accords for Peace and Prosperity. Africa Intelligence reported that the two sides were expected to meet, although Al Jazeera has been unable to independently confirm the gathering.

At the heart of the impasse are two commitments: neutralising the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) and Rwanda lifting its defensive measures. The governments disagree not only over progress on these obligations but also on what would constitute compliance.

The Washington Accords, signed on December 4, 2025, build on the peace agreement signed by the two governments on June 27, 2025, and the Declaration of Principles of April 25, 2025.

The commitments include neutralising the FDLR, Rwanda’s disengagement of forces and the lifting of defensive measures, respect for territorial integrity, and an end to support for armed groups.

Implementation is overseen by the Joint Security Coordination Mechanism (JSCM), which includes representatives of the DRC, Rwanda, the United States, Qatar, Togo in its role as African Union mediator, and the AU Commission. The mechanism coordinates security measures, including efforts to locate the FDLR.

The JSCM has held several rounds of meetings, but progress has largely focused on procedures, monitoring and verification rather than resolving the central disagreement.

At meetings in July, August and September 2026, the parties discussed the security situation in eastern DRC, information-sharing, monitoring arrangements and the disarmament and demobilisation of FDLR members. They also considered ways to strengthen verification. However, they have yet to agree on what would constitute fulfilment of their respective security obligations.

Rwanda says it has begun implementing its commitments. Addressing the United Nations Security Council on September 29 , Rwanda’s Permanent Representative, Martin Ngoga, said Kigali had started lifting its defensive measures.

He maintained, however, that the FDLR remained active in eastern DRC and continued to cooperate with Congolese forces and other armed groups. Rwanda considers ending this alleged cooperation essential to implementing the agreement.

Kinshasa, meanwhile, points to its efforts to disarm and demobilise FDLR fighters. On July 28 , the Congolese government announced a protocol with a faction of the armed wing of the FDLR, setting out arrangements for disarmament and demobilisation.

Government spokesman Patrick Muyaya told Al Jazeera that the process formed part of the commitments under the Washington agreements.

Rwanda rejected the arrangement. Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe called it a “crude manipulation”, while Ngoga argued that an agreement with one faction could not satisfy the broader commitment to neutralise the group.

The disagreement exposes the central problem: Kinshasa presents the protocol as progress towards neutralisation, while Kigali argues that disarming one faction does not demonstrate that the FDLR’s wider operational capacity has been dismantled. The parties have yet to establish a shared standard for measuring progress.

Why did the US sanction Rwanda’s Ministry of Defence?

On October 28 , the US sanctioned Rwanda’s Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Rwandan financial institution, over alleged support for the M23 armed group in eastern DRC.

Washington accused the ministry of directing Rwandan forces operating alongside M23 and providing the group with military equipment and other assistance. It also alleged that Zigama facilitated financial and logistical support for Rwanda’s military activities.

The US Treasury said the sanctions were intended to hold Rwanda accountable for its commitments under the Washington Accords.

Kigali rejected the allegations. Government spokesperson Yolande Makolo said the commitments concerning the FDLR remained unfulfilled and called for all parties to be held accountable.

The sanctions increased pressure on Rwanda and underscored Washington’s determination to push for implementation of the agreement it helped broker.

How do the talks with M23 fit into the process?

The Washington Accords address security commitments between Rwanda and the DRC. However, negotiations between Kinshasa, M23 and its ally, the Congo River Alliance (AFC), follow a separate track facilitated by Qatar under the Doha process.

The two tracks are distinct but connected. The June 2025 peace agreement recognises that resolving the conflict in eastern DRC also requires addressing non-state armed groups.

The Doha process produced a Declaration of Principles in July 2025 and a framework for a comprehensive peace agreement covering ceasefire monitoring, humanitarian access, security arrangements, disarmament and the restoration of state authority.

The political landscape shifted on October 12, 2026, when the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) was established. The new movement was presented as replacing the AFC/M23 political-military structure and bringing together its political and military components. In its founding declaration, the FRN announced the dissolution of the AFC and said it would assume the coalition’s rights and obligations, including commitments under the Doha process.

Although M23’s political and military leadership has been incorporated into the new structure, the founding declaration does not explicitly spell out the separate organisational status of the armed movement. The distinction between M23 as an armed movement and the broader political-military coalition remains important, particularly in determining who represents the nongovernmental side in the Doha negotiations and who is responsible for implementing commitments made under that process.

What is the minerals partnership between Washington and Kinshasa?

Alongside the peace agreement, the US and the DRC signed a strategic partnership on December 4, 2025, to expand economic cooperation, including investment in mining, critical minerals and infrastructure.

The partnership reflects Washington’s interest in the DRC’s copper and cobalt reserves and efforts to diversify mineral supply chains. Following a steering committee meeting in Paris on November 6 , the two governments reported growing interest from US companies. Kinshasa has stressed that the partnership should be judged by tangible investments rather than announcements.

The Washington process follows decades of efforts to address conflict in eastern DRC and tensions between the two neighbours.

The 1999 Lusaka Ceasefire Agreement sought to end the Second Congo War and provide for the withdrawal of foreign forces and disarmament of armed groups. Among those groups were remnants of the former Rwandan armed forces and members of the Interahamwe militia who fled to the DRC after the 1994 genocide against Tutsi in Rwanda. Elements of these forces later formed the FDLR, established in 2000.

The 2002 Pretoria Agreement committed Rwanda to withdrawing its troops from the DRC, while Kinshasa undertook to address the presence of former Rwandan armed forces and Interahamwe elements. The 2007 Nairobi Communique and the 2013 Peace, Security and Cooperation Framework renewed commitments to disarm armed groups, respect territorial integrity and strengthen regional cooperation.

Those initiatives struggled to overcome mutual security concerns and the continued presence of armed groups. The FDLR remains a central point of contention nearly three decades after its origins in eastern DRC.

The next round of talks will test whether Kigali and Kinshasa can move beyond competing interpretations of their obligations and agree on a credible, verifiable process for implementing the Washington Accords. Without agreement on how compliance is measured, progress on the ground risks lagging far behind the diplomatic framework.

articles.title: Intense flooding slams Florida from a developing storm that could snarl early Thanksgiving travel on the East Coast
articles.summary: Torrential rainfall and severe flooding shut roads and forced water rescues in southeast Florida as a multiday flood threat unfolds along the state’s Atlantic coast.
articles.body: Torrential rainfall and severe flooding shut down roads, gushed into homes and forced high-water rescues in southeast Florida overnight as a multiday flood threat unfolds along the state’s Atlantic coast. ⛈️ ☔️ Track the storm and get your local forecast in the CNN Weather app. Parts of the northern Miami metro area, including Broward County, suffered the most significant rainfall. Over a foot of rain — more than three Novembers’ worth — fell in mere hours in the Hollywood area, with some places getting walloped by more than 5 inches of rain per hour, the National Weather Service in Miami said. Hollywood’s mayor declared a state of emergency and urged residents to shelter in place as the torrent closed parts of Interstate 95 and Florida’s Turnpike. First responders received more than 300 calls for service between 11 p.m. and 4 a.m., the Hollywood Police Department said, and high-water vehicles were still deployed late Wednesday morning. The ferocious rainfall also caused the roof to collapse at the Temple Sinai in Hollywood, police said. No injuries were reported. The deluge has also forced schools to shutter, including several campuses of Keiser University. All Broward County Public Schools were closed Wednesday, and the status of Thursday’s classes “will be shared later today,” the school district said. Extreme rainfall like this is becoming more frequent as the world warms due to fossil fuel pollution. A warmer atmosphere can soak up more moisture like a sponge and wring it out in the form of gushing rainfall. More flash flooding is possible in southeast Florida over the next few days, but the biggest area of concern will shift north and include parts of the Space Coast that were inundated with historic rainfall and severe flooding earlier this month. Some rivers are still high in those areas and vulnerable to flooding from the additional rain. Winds blowing onshore and high surf will also pound the Florida coast in coming days, producing dangerous rip currents and potentially major beach erosion. After drenching Florida, this budding storm will head north, where it’s likely to throw a wrench in travel during the busy pre-Thanksgiving weekend. It will linger off the Southeast coast until Saturday, when it’ll begin to push farther north. The storm’s East Coast impacts into early next week will depend on its path, which forecast models are still working to suss out. Florida’s multiday deluge Florida’s eastern coast faces three consecutive days of a Level 3 out of 4 flood risk through Friday. A widespread 3 to 6 inches of rain is expected to fall across eastern Florida through Friday, with 8 to 12 inches or more possible in some areas along the state’s eastern coast. A foot of rain in some locations, like Daytona Beach, would mean four Novembers’ worth of rain fell in just a few days. Pinpointing the exact communities that might endure those higher-end totals is challenging and will depend on where storms form and stall out with torrential rain for several hours. Melbourne, Florida – the epicenter of the historic rainfall earlier this month – is in the highest flood threat area on Wednesday and Thursday. The city just had its rainiest day on record on November 2 after 11.5 inches fell there. Melbourne is about 8 inches shy of its rainiest year on record, which could happen during this week’s storm. On Friday, the Level 3 of 4 flood risk stretches farther north to near the Florida-Georgia state line, as seen in purple below. Here, rainfall rates greater than 2 inches an hour are possible, which would add significantly to rainfall totals from the two previous days and increase the chances for serious flooding. Wetter than normal periods are not a surprise in Florida this fall and winter as the super El Niño continues to strengthen, changing global weather patterns and increasing storm chances across the US Southeast. Holiday travel threat could emerge Forecast models are still sorting out exactly where the storm will go after Florida, but there are two favored scenarios at this time, both of which could impact travel starting this weekend. Last year, the weekend prior to Thanksgiving was one of the busiest travel periods of the holiday week, according to TSA screening data. Scenario 1: The storm tracks near or into the Southeast coast this weekend and then darts into the Northeast by Monday, bringing a sloppy mix of rain, wind and possibly coastal flooding with it. This track could cause airport delays and create treacherous travel on roads, including along the parts of highly traveled Interstate 95. Scenario 2: The storm stays along the the Southeast coast, delivering rain, wind and coastal flooding to the region before heading out to sea, minimizing its impacts farther north along the East Coast. Right now, it’s looking like the first scenario is most likely, but that could change as the forecast comes into focus later this week. There’s also a low chance the system could eventually transition into a subtropical storm if it remains over water long enough, according to the National Hurricane Center. Subtropical storms share some characteristics with tropical systems like hurricanes, including drawing energy from warm ocean water. But they also have features of non-tropical storms, like the systems that move across the country year-round. The distinction makes little difference when it comes to impacts: They bring strong winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. The storm would be named Kyle if it becomes subtropical. CNN’s Hanna Park contributed to this report.

articles.title: Xi, Putin condemn sanctions as Trump arrives in China
articles.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin condemned U.S. sanctions against their countries Wednesday, as they prepare for a rare trilateral meeting with President Trump. Speaking at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China, Xi said Beijing would cut tariffs and promote free trade, a contrast to Trump’s global trade war that…
articles.body:
Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin condemned U.S. sanctions against their countries Wednesday, as they prepare for a rare trilateral meeting with President Trump.

Speaking at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China, Xi said Beijing would cut tariffs and promote free trade, a contrast to Trump’s global trade war that directly hit China during both of his terms in office.

“We must firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system with the World Trade Organization at its core, support ​free and open trade and investment,” Xi told the APEC audience, according to Reuters .

Trump has repeatedly targeted China with steep import taxes, accusing them of allowing their cheap goods to flood U.S. markets and hurt American businesses. After his initial tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court, he levied additional sanctions against the country. And as a key ally of Iran , Beijing has been a target of U.S. efforts to choke out the regime’s economy.

For Putin, western sanctions were a focus of his speech. The Russian leader decried sanctions and tariffs, saying they have “lost their intimidating effect,” according to The Associated Press .

Russia has been a target of U.S. economic penalties since it launched its war in Ukraine nearly five years ago. Washington and Kyiv maintained a close partnership under the Biden administration, though Trump has been far more critical of Ukraine and its leader Volodymyr Zelensky. The president has also maintained a closer relationship with Putin than his predecessor.

In an attempt to curb high fuel prices at home tied to the Iran war, Trump waived tariffs on Russian diesel and made a deal with Moscow to purchase it, Critics — including some Republicans — blasted the move as funding Russia’s war.

After the presidents traded jabs indirectly, Xi, Putin and Trump are set to meet face to face in China for the first-ever trilateral meeting between the three leaders.

Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac in China early Wednesday, a rare move but a return of the gesture that the commander in chief offered to him during his visit to Washington earlier this year. Trump also shook hands with Putin after arriving at the APEC banquet Wednesday.

The trio are expected to discuss a range of issues during the summit, including the wars in Ukraine and Iran, tariffs, artificial intelligence and more. Though it is not clear what, if any, tangible accomplishments will come out of the meeting.
