articles.title: Putin loves peace talks — here’s how to make him love peace
articles.summary: After recent diplomatic efforts in Abu Dhabi failed to produce a ceasefire, critics argue that the United States should prioritize substantial, performance-based military aid to Ukraine to force a Russian withdrawal.
articles.body:
Of all things in the world, Russian President Vladimir Putin, a wanted war criminal , adores peace talks the most. Not peace, mind you — peace talks. He finds them irresistible, the way an arsonist gets giddy over a fire-safety seminar.

Last week, all eyes were on Abu Dhabi, as if a shortage of meetings were the problem. What was bizarrely described as “peace negotiations” looked more like an imitation of an imitation. Moscow performing diplomacy, Washington performing mediation. But, thankfully, one real outcome emerged: a promised prisoner swap .

The rest floated unencumbered by basic facts. Russia invaded Ukraine. The aggressor can end the war any day it chooses by going home. Ukraine is already doing everything and more for peace, but it cannot secure it by signing on some dotted line.

The courage of Ukrainian soldiers is the reason Russia’s war has yet to engulf the rest of Europe — including allies America is bound by treaty to defend.

Instead of discussing how to end the war, Moscow came up with yet another sleight of hand, a need to revisit European security architecture .

The claim that NATO threatens Russia is a fabrication the Kremlin happily spreads but doesn’t actually believe. When Finland joined the alliance in 2023, adding 830 miles to NATO’s border with Russia, Moscow responded by sending some 80 percent of its troops on that frontier to fight in Ukraine.

On the eve of the talks, the Ukrainian military reported a new record from the front: 3,000 enemy combatants killed or seriously wounded in a single day. As NATO’s Secretary General Mark Rutte put it : Russia loses nearly as many troops each month as the U.S. lost over 14 years in Vietnam.

Security guarantees for the aggressor is the level of absurdity Moscow is aiming for, knowing that such demands can’t be met by definition. Though, one thing Putin refuses to discuss is a ceasefire — the necessary precondition for peace.

It took Ukraine all of 24 hours to accept an unconditional ceasefire in March 2025. Russia still hasn’t.

In Abu Dhabi, the Kremlin’s chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, restated Russia’s eliminationist agenda: “every inch of Russian land will be returned to Russia, one way or another.” What does that even mean? Russia signed its name to Ukraine’s borders twice, in 1994 and 1997.

Picture a violent burglar who breaks into a family’s home, kills two of the five children, takes the room where they slept and announces he lives there now. A mediator arrives and, no joke, invites the family to sit down with the murderer to discuss security concerns of both sides.

Importantly, he is also the main danger to himself: breaking into homes is how criminals get hurt. Security for Russia begins with accountability, the kind that turns a country’s governing priorities from a fixation on invading neighbors to an effort to offer Russian people better — freer and more prosperous — lives.

Regrettably, Steve Witkoff has a different word for the homicidal maniac. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” he told Putin in St. Petersburg last month. Oleksandra Matviichuk, who won the Nobel Peace Prize for documenting Russian war crimes, never tires of repeating: occupation is not peace, it is just another form of war. Pressuring Ukraine to accept Russian occupation, or worse yet, to cede territory Kyiv currently controls, is the opposite of progress toward peace.

On Nov. 12, as American envoys flew from Abu Dhabi to Moscow to meet with Putin, Zelensky posted about a disturbing battlefield development: “our units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield’s operations over the territory of Ukraine for several days now.”

Diplomacy deserves a chance, but it must be judged by results. Talks that produce no ceasefire have costs. They erode Washington’s credibility and delay the exercise of American power that could compel Moscow to wind down its war. Where is that peace through strength Trump promised two years ago?

Americans overwhelmingly support Ukraine and despise Russia. Come January, the new Congress will have a chance to turn that sentiment into a win both houses and both parties can claim. Why not make $10 billion in weapons for Ukraine the first legislative priority? Write the law so that four months later, another $20 billion follows automatically. Four months after that, $30 billion, then $50 billion every year. Before each tranche, one test applies: is Russia still firing at Ukraine? If yes, the aid flows. If the guns fall silent, it stops.

Congress has done this before . In 2017, it voted almost unanimously to bar any president from easing Russia sanctions without its review.

For America’s $32 trillion economy, this is a rounding error. Fifty billion dollars a year comes to a fraction of a fraction of one percent of GDP. In a world where Russia’s appetite for violent revanchism isn’t curbed, the war spreads west, and the Pentagon’s trillion-dollar budget has to double or triple . That would be like passing a $50 billion package every single week.

Why do this? So Moscow learns that aggression is doomed to fail, that America will keep the promise it made in 1994, when it talked Ukraine out of the world’s third-largest nuclear arsenal . There’s a lesson the world should under no circumstances learn: give up your nukes and you get invaded. If that sticks, kiss nonproliferation goodbye. The whole planet turns into a house of dynamite.

As the Abu Dhabi talks concluded, Russian drones killed two people in Odesa and set a Kyiv hospital ablaze, forcing patients on crutches and in wheelchairs to flee. A bill moving through Congress could achieve what two days of negotiations could not: make the Kremlin want peace instead of reveling in peace talks.

Andrew Chakhoyan is an academic director at the University of Amsterdam. He previously served in the U.S. government at the Millennium Challenge Corporation and studied at Harvard Kennedy School and Donetsk State Tech University.

articles.title: What is the ‘endgame’ in Syria, as Israeli rivals look for new government?
articles.summary: As Israel intensifies its incursions into southern Syria, analysts say there will be little change in the future.
articles.body:
As Israel’s post-election political scenario continues to unfold, analysts and experts tell Al Jazeera that Israel’s occupation of parts of southern Syria is likely to continue regardless of who becomes the country’s next prime minister.

Israeli incursions and raids in the provinces of Quneitra and Deraa intensified in recent weeks as Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and de facto leader of the opposition Gadi Eisenkot try to form a new government.

Since the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024, Israel has occupied key strategic points in southern Syria, such as Jabal al-Sheikh, which Israelis know as Mount Hermon.

Israel’s continued violations of Syrian sovereignty are piling pressure on the new government led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa in Damascus, which has been targeted in Israeli air strikes . Syria has sought to harness its deepening ties with regional and international powers to pressure Israel to stop its incursions, but this strategy does not yet appear to be bearing fruit.

Israeli raids, often resulting in detentions or civilian deaths, are leading to continued instability in southern Syria, which has already suffered from the 14-year war between al-Assad’s forces and the opposition. But even with a prospective change in government in Israel following last month’s election, the endgame has not changed for Israel, analysts say.

“Israel appears to want both to dematerialise the south and the freedom to intervene there,” Navvar Saban, a researcher in security and military affairs at the Arab Center for Contemporary Syrian Studies in Damascus, told Al Jazeera.

“Israel is turning its military presence into an established reality before any settlement. Repeated incursions, checkpoints, construction, [are all] strengthening its control and negotiation leverage.”

Syrians in areas close to the Israeli occupation of their land live in a constant state of fear, with homes being raided and civilians being arrested. The fate of 35 Syrians detained by Israel is still unknown, according to a report by the Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR).

Israeli forces have also conducted a series of air and artillery strikes on villages and countryside in southern Syria, with 69 people killed since 2024, the SNHR report said.

On Tuesday, a video emerged of an Israeli raid in the province of Deraa , one of the areas heavily targeted by Israel.

Israeli forces left a local home with bullet holes in the window, walls charred with soot, and belongings tossed across the floor. Locals and experts say Israeli troops routinely raid homes and detain residents in the area, while Syrian authorities appear powerless to prevent them.

Israel has occupied the Golan Heights since 1967 and illegally annexed the strategic Syrian territory in 1981. In December 2024, during the collapse of the al-Assad regime, Israel invaded and occupied neutral areas of the Golan, along with more Syrian lands. Over the next year, Syria was attacked more than 600 times , despite the new government in Damascus saying it posed no threat to Israel.

For the past two years, Syria’s stated priorities have mostly been internal. The new government has worked to remove international sanctions and spur a stuttering local economy . Internationally, Syria has said it wants no problems with its neighbours and has tried to reintegrate the country into the regional fold after years of broken relations under al-Assad.

But since October 2023, when the genocide in Gaza began, Israel has adopted a more outwardly aggressive strategy with its neighbours, including Lebanon and Syria. In recent months, Israel has been intensifying its incursions and raids on southern Syria in particular.

A report published in late October by the Arab Reform Initiative found that Israel had conducted 678 ground incursions and 168 raids into southern Syria between January and September 2026. In September alone, it launched 113 incursions, 27 raids and 24 artillery shelling incidents into southern Syria, showing what the report called “a trend toward escalation”.

Due to the situation, government officials have been prevented from performing their duties in many parts of southern Syria, effectively putting these areas under Israeli security control. Syrians arrested by Israeli forces have recounted brutal prison conditions, including physical and psychological abuse.

Externally, this is the biggest “challenge for al-Sharaa and his government” Issam al-Reis, a senior military adviser and research director at Damascus-based nonprofit Etana Syria, told Al Jazeera.

“Everything else could be solved, including Suwayda and the integration of the SDF, but the truth is this is the biggest concern to the government,” he said, referring to the Syrian Democratic Forces, officially dissolved in August.

Israeli elections last month came with the prospect of a new government.

Matan Kahana was elected parliament speaker on Tuesday , in a blow to the prospect of Netanyahu returning to power. He is an ally of Eisenkot, the Yashar party leader invited to form the next government to replace Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving premier.

But analysts say even if Eisenkot succeeds and forms a government, there will be few changes in Israel’s policy on Syria.

“The [Israeli] government could change their diplomatic approach, but I would not assume it would abandon Israel’s security demands or withdraw automatically,” researcher Saban said. “The security demands for the Israelis will never change. The ratio of it might change, the approach might change. But the security demand is always present in the Israeli mentality.”

Al-Reis, who is also a former military officer who defected from the Syrian Army, said decisions taken by Israel in southern Syria are dictated by military matters and not political concerns.

“Therefore, it will not change as a result of the electoral government change,” he said.

Even Israeli soldiers who have taken part in the occupation of southern Syria have said they are unconvinced by the army and the government’s narrative that southern Syria poses a security concern to Israel.

“The feeling [is] that there’s some bluff everybody is playing along with. We’re there, so we need to invent a story that it’s dangerous,” one soldier told the Israeli daily Haaretz.

Without a clear policy or mission, troops fire at civilians, shoot at animals, or conduct night-time searches during which families are pulled from their beds, detained and questioned, similar to Israeli conduct in the occupied West Bank.

Israel has claimed it is in southern Syria to counter groups opposed to Iran operating in the territory, although since the fall of the al-Assad government, Iran-linked militias have been withdrawn.

Still, since then it has at various times alleged that the ISIL (ISIS) group and Lebanon’s branch of the Muslim Brotherhood are present in Syria, although the latter denies it operates outside Lebanon’s borders.

Saban said, because many residents of southern Deraa and Quneitra are farmers, guns are present in the region, but this is far from the narrative painted by the Israeli military.

“It’s a weaponised culture [because] they are farmers with herds, but resistance to incursion is not automatically evidence of an organised, externally directed network,” he said. “The Israelis are trying to project that the whole area is an organised resistance. But there isn’t any organised resistance. People having arms over there does not mean that they are part of a network.”

Saban believes that Israel’s presence and endgame in southern Syria are less about beating back the so-called resistance and more about creating a new reality on the ground. This is one in which the Israeli military can operate freely without opposition from locals or the Syrian government.

“It is clear that there is no intention at all to withdraw from Syrian territory,” al-Reis said.

articles.title: Can the US and Iran sustain a ‘frozen war’?
articles.summary: Tehran may eventually decide that ‘escalating confrontation’ is preferable to status quo, says analyst Hamidreza Azizi.
articles.body:
For months, Iran and the United States have been weighing a return to outright war over persevering towards a negotiated peace. But they appear to have settled on something in between.

While largely stopping short of full-blown military confrontation since July, when a June Memorandum of Understanding between the two sides fell apart , the two countries have instead intermittently traded attacks while using what economic levers they have to inflict as much pain as possible on the other side. Both have maintained blockades in and around the Strait of Hormuz, once the conduit for one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas supplies.

In recent days, Iran says it has targeted US military sites in Bahrain and Kuwait , while the US has carried out an air strike on Iran’s Qeshm island on Tuesday.

Iran has, meanwhile, continued to target ships it says have not followed its rules for passing through the critical Hormuz strait, as the US stands firm on its economic sanctions and naval blockade of Iran’s ports.

The result, if not precisely a frozen conflict , is certainly demonstrating a pattern of limited confrontation that could carry on for months without escalating into all-out war, analysts say. But sustaining this status quo would mean absorbing mounting economic and political costs that could eventually prove untenable for either side, but especially for Iran, they say.

“The two sides have very different calculations about the costs of prolonging the confrontation,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera. “As economic pressure mounts, Iran may become increasingly willing to take military risks to break the deadlock.”

US President Donald Trump’s administration has appeared to shift gears on Iran following the ruling Republicans’ crushing defeat by the opposition Democratic Party in this month’s midterm elections , which both Trump and his Vice President JD Vance have acknowledged the deeply unpopular Iran war was partly to blame for.

Last week, Trump said the war was “effectively over” militarily, though he also warned that he “would not hesitate” to resume strikes if diplomacy failed.

Meanwhile, Trump’s Secretary of State Marco Rubio has suggested the US is pursuing economic pressure rather than military pressure.

“We don’t need to conduct military strikes if we’re achieving the same objective through economic means and economic pressure,” Rubio said last week. “The economic pressure on Iran is going to get even worse.”

But this plan to maintain an uneasy standoff with Iran while avoiding a return to full-blown war may not sit well in Tehran, where Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has told officials to end the state of “neither war nor peace”.

“We will not remain in a state of ‘neither war nor peace,” Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and top negotiator, told parliament on Sunday. “It makes absolutely no difference to us whether the United States wants negotiations or war.”’

The economic pain of a frozen conflict would be extensive for Iran, the Gulf and the global economy, analysts say.

Iran’s disruptions to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have already triggered some of the most dramatic fluctuations in the oil price in years.

In late October, Brent crude, the world’s crude oil benchmark, was trading at $117 per barrel, its highest price since April when it reached a four-year high. The price, which was about $72 just before the war began, has since fallen back to $92 per barrel as vessels brave the Strait of Hormuz, despite an uptick in attacks . But that is still 30 percent higher than before the war.

Petrol and diesel prices in the US have trended similarly. The current average for petrol is $3.80 per gallon (3.8 litres), the lowest since March, but that is still a far cry from the pre-war average of $2.98, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).

The average price for diesel stands at just over $5.93 per gallon as of November 17, 2026, according to the US Energy Information Administration. That compares with $3.72 in February before the war began, and has taken a particular toll on farmers and truckers in the US – many of whom form the backbone of Trump’s MAGA support base.

Ron Bousso, a columnist who analyses global energy markets for Reuters, said he estimates that a drawn-out, low-grade conflict between the US and Iran could “put a floor under oil prices” and force Gulf oil exporters to keep contending with massive freight and insurance costs.

The danger, he wrote for Reuters last week, “⁠is not simply another dramatic surge in oil prices caused by renewed war. It is that the Middle East settles into something more durable and more insidious: a conflict intense enough to keep shipping dangerous, insurance expensive and energy infrastructure vulnerable, but contained enough for the world to learn to live with it.”

Such a scenario would mean longer-term economic strain on many of the US’s Gulf allies, while, according to Bousso, global energy disruption becomes the “new normal”.

The economic toll on Iran could be even more severe, however.

Week after week, the US has introduced more sanctions against not only Iranian entities, but entities it says are trading with or connected to Iran , further isolating the country from the outside world. Meanwhile, the US naval blockade has made it increasingly difficult for Iran to export its oil.

As a result, Iran’s government has continuously prioritised “short-term survival” over much-needed sustainable investment at a time when its economy is shrinking and its people are dealing with one of the world’s highest inflation rates, Mohammad Farzanegan, professor of Middle East economics at the interdisciplinary Center for Near and Middle Eastern Studies, told Al Jazeera.

Iran’s falling oil revenues, he said, “have introduced significant pressure on the government budget, increasing the need to raise taxes, reduce subsidies, especially on energy products, and plan painful economic reforms”.

“All these developments have amplified the feeling of deprivation among the population, especially the youth,” Farzanegan added.

Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst and affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies, agreed that “Iran’s population is suffering tremendously”, saying “they bear the brunt of this economic war”.

“While this is not sustainable, long term the question is, if it can hold until Trump leaves office,” Parsi told Al Jazeera.

The economic pressure on Iran also risks triggering political upheaval, according to Azizi and Farzanegan.

“The [Iranian] leadership is particularly concerned about the possibility of renewed domestic unrest at a time when it is confronting the United States externally,” said Azizi. “Allowing the current situation to continue indefinitely could gradually weaken the economy, increase domestic instability and undermine the government’s position.”

Farzanegan said that any new major shock, such as a natural or human-made disaster, “could ignite a new round of violent protests”.

How long Iran can maintain the status quo hinges on the extent to which it can find ways to bypass the blockade, secure alternative trade partners and tame corruption and domestic economic grievances, he said. “It is unclear how long the government can maintain stability inside Iran under such fragile economic conditions,” he added.

Will the US or Iran deliberately escalate?

There are political costs to a drawn-out conflict for the US, too.

For one, it goes against one of Trump’s core campaign pledges – no new foreign wars. Maintaining the status quo keeps alive a conflict that more than 70 percent of Americans say they want to end, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll on November 9.

“There is also the question of credibility,” said Azizi. “The United States has demonstrated its overwhelming military superiority, but it has so far been unable to compel Iran to abandon its control over the strait or accept Washington’s terms. The longer this situation continues, the more difficult it becomes to explain what the American strategy is ultimately supposed to achieve.”

As a result, analysts say, there are reasons that both Iran and the US could choose to escalate, triggering a return to war.

Iran’s government, said Azizi, “may eventually conclude that deliberately escalating the confrontation is preferable to allowing its economic and strategic position to deteriorate further”.

Trump’s blistering midterm election defeat, on the other hand, has “removed the last consideration we all thought would hold him back from a full-scale war”, said Parsi.

Trump still has the option of letting sanctions run their course, he added, but if he comes to believe that another military attack “will spell the end of the Islamic republic, or simply wants revenge, this ‘not-peace’ could easily become a full war”.

articles.title: Trump meets longtime friend Imelda Marcos while visiting son in Philippines
articles.summary: President Trump visited his longtime friend Imelda Marcos in the Philippines Wednesday before heading to China for a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Marcos is the widow of longtime Philippine dictator Ferdinand Marcos Sr., and the mother of the now-president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr. A video posted to social…
articles.body:
President Trump visited his longtime friend Imelda Marcos in the Philippines Wednesday before heading to China for a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Marcos is the widow of longtime Philippine dictator Ferdinand Marcos Sr., and the mother of the now-president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

A video posted to social platform X by a White House aide shows Trump and Marcos, now 97 and in a wheelchair, exchanging pleasantries during his visit. She can also be seen blowing him a kiss.

“She’s always the most beautiful,” the president said in a separate video .

Trump visited Manila and met with Marcos Jr., who rolled out the red carpet for the U.S. leader, even sending him Jollibee fried chicken, a Philippine fast-food specialty, for a late-night snack.

The two countries reached a new trade deal to benefit farmers and the energy industry, Trump said Wednesday on Truth Social, but did not elaborate.

Marcos has maintained a good relationship with the Trump administration over the years. After Trump secured another term in 2024, Marcos Jr. phoned the president to congratulate him on his victory and sent his mother’s congratulations.

The two met while partying in New York during her time as first lady, when she was known for her style and expansive shoe collection despite leading a country in economic collapse. Marcos Sr. was eventually ousted in a military coup in the late 1980s and fled to Hawaii.

But even in the U.S., Marcos faced prosecution over accusations that she stole Philippine money and invested it in the U.S. The former first lady was acquitted on all charges in the 1990s, according to The New York Times.

Upon Marcos Sr.’s death, his widow returned to the Philippines and ultimately ran for Congress, but not without legal challenges. She was convicted on charges of corruption in 1993, which the Philippine Supreme Court overturned in 1998, the Times reported.

Marcos was found guilty on additional corruption charges in 2018, which the Supreme Court overturned earlier this year, per the Canadian Inquirer.

articles.title: Israeli tanks roll into central Gaza in first ground operation since ceasefire began
articles.summary: Israeli tanks advanced in an area of ​the central Gaza Strip, witnesses said, and the Israeli military said its forces were targeting Hamas infrastructure.
articles.body: Israeli tanks advanced in an area of ​the central Gaza Strip on Wednesday, witnesses said, and the Israeli military said its forces were targeting Hamas infrastructure outside areas that Israel controls in ⁠the enclave. Witnesses said some Israeli tanks rolled onto the main Salahudeen road, west of the Yellow Line that marks the boundary of the two-thirds of the Gaza Strip still under Israeli control despite ⁠a ceasefire that has ​lasted more ⁠than a year. An Israeli airstrike near the army raid killed one person, Palestinian medics said. The medics ⁠said separate Israeli airstrikes had killed two other people ​earlier ⁠in the day in ‌Deir al-Balah and Gaza City. An Israeli military spokesperson told NBC News that the military was carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of ‌the Yellow Line in central Gaza ‌and that it had struck a militant in southern Gaza earlier on Wednesday. The lates confirmed that it was the first ground operation since the U.S. brokered ceasefire came into effect in October 2025. The truce halted major fighting in the Israel-Gaza war although it has not stopped Israeli attacks or secured Hamas’ disarmament. The spokesperson had no immediate comment on other strikes. Israel, which says Hamas has recently been regrouping and rearming, has stepped up attacks against the Islamist group. articles.title: Protesters call for regime change in Iran following deadly crash that killed 13 oil and gas workers
articles.summary: Hundreds take to the streets in western Iran after 13 oil workers are killed, with demonstrations escalating into political protests against Tehran's leadership.
articles.body: Hundreds of protesters poured into the streets of western Iran on Tuesday following a deadly bus crash that killed 13 oil and gas workers, with demonstrations quickly escalating into anti-government chants with some protesters calling for the return of the Pahlavi monarchy. The unrest erupted in Abdanan, a city in Iran's Ilam province near the Iraqi border, where residents initially gathered to demand accountability for Saturday's fatal accident before turning their anger toward the Islamic Republic's leadership. Videos obtained by Fox News Digital showed large crowds marching through the streets, chanting "Death to the dictator!" IRANIAN PROTESTER HANGED HOURS AFTER MARRYING HIS IMPRISONED FIANCÉE OVER JAIL PHONE LINE Iranian-American journalist and foreign policy analyst Lisa Daftari said the demonstrations underscore the deeper political tensions facing Tehran. "Abdanan is a reminder that the Islamic Republic sits on top of a dormant volcano," Daftari told Fox News Digital. "These uprisings start with different catalysts, and in this case it was a local grievance, but they always arrive at the same conclusion." "The slogans we hear are ‘Death to the Dictator’ and ‘Javid Shah,’ not complaints about a policy. They are an indictment of the entire system, top to bottom," she said. New reports Wednesday indicated that Iranian security forces arrested at least seven people, including a 15-year-old boy, during the unrest in Abdanan. The Hengaw Organization for Human Rights said two detainees had been released, but the whereabouts of five others remained unknown. The Kurdistan Human Rights Network separately reported that security forces fired tear gas at demonstrators and that internet access was disrupted during the crackdown. Iran's Revolutionary Guard-affiliated Fars news agency acknowledged the demonstrations, reporting that approximately 200 to 300 people initially gathered in Abdanan's Vali-e Asr Square before the crowd grew to roughly 1,000. Fars reported that the slogans initially focused on the deadly accident but subsequently took on a political character. Police were deployed as protesters moved into surrounding streets, according to AFP's Nov. 17 report. ONE GLARING ISSUE GOES UNADDRESSED IN UN CHIEF'S HIGH-STAKES TALKS WITH IRAN'S PRESIDENT The protests followed Saturday's overturning of a bus transporting workers from the Dehloran gas processing project. Thirteen people were killed and more than a dozen injured, according to Iranian media reports. Euronews Persian reported on Nov. 17 that provincial traffic police identified driver negligence, irregularities involving the company's bus contract and inadequate road barriers as factors contributing to the accident. Prosecutors have announced legal proceedings against the company and provincial transportation officials, although responsibility has not been established in court. Authorities warned against allowing the demonstrations to escalate. "Individuals who seek to exploit this incident to disrupt public order or incite public sentiment will be dealt with firmly," Abdanan prosecutor Amrollah Misaie said, according to Iran's judiciary-affiliated Mizan news agency, as quoted by AFP on Nov. 17. Daftari, The Foreign Desk editor-in-chief, argued that the Iranian government's greatest challenge may ultimately come from within, regardless of its confrontation with Washington and Jerusalem. "Whatever happens in the military standoff with the United States and Israel, Tehran will still face its most serious adversary at home," she said. She also pointed to the protesters' willingness to return to the streets following the deadly crackdown earlier this year, saying that "despite thousands being killed by the regime for protesting in January, we still see bravery on the part of the Iranian people to tell the world of their grievances and to stand up to their murderers." At the United Nations' daily briefing on Tuesday, Fox News Digital asked the U.N. spokesperson whether the organization was monitoring the situation, particularly the actions of Iranian security forces on the ground. "Well, we're keeping an eye on the situation and we want to make sure that all peaceful protests are allowed to proceed without obstruction and without harassment of protesters," the spokesperson said and added, "Certainly our human rights colleagues will continue to monitor the situation as we've done in the past." IRAN TURNS CITIZENS INTO INFORMANTS AS CHILLING CRACKDOWN SPREADS BEYOND ITS BORDERS The demonstrations carry particular significance because Abdanan was previously a flashpoint during Iran's nationwide anti-government protests earlier this year. Reuters reported on Jan. 9 that it had verified footage showing demonstrators marching through the city during the broader uprising against the Islamic Republic. The city also witnessed renewed tensions during mourning ceremonies for protesters killed in the January unrest. Reuters reported on Feb. 18 that witnesses and activists said security forces opened fire on hundreds of mourners gathered at a cemetery in Abdanan. articles.body: Hundreds of Iranians took to the streets chanting "Death to the dictator!" and other anti-government messages in the wake of a deadly bus crash over the weekend that killed 13 employees of an oil refinery company, reports said. The rare display of anti-government anger unfolded Tuesday in Abdanan, a city in western Iran near the country's border with Iraq. "Those who seek to exploit this incident to disrupt public order and inflame people’s emotions will be dealt with decisively," local prosecutor Amrollah Meysaei was quoted by Iran's Mizan news agency as saying, according to Radio Free Europe. The outlet, citing Iran's Fars news agency, also reported that an estimated 1,000 people took part in the protests, making them the largest demonstrations since mass unrest swept across Iran at the beginning of this year. A video shared by HRANA, a rights group based outside Iran, also showed a crowd of protesters marching through the center of Abdanan, calling for accountability for the road accident. articles.title: Peltola win doesn’t end DOJ scrutiny of Alaska Senate race, officials say
articles.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola was declared the victor in Alaska’s Senate race Tuesday, but Justice Department officials say their interest in the contentious campaig...
articles.body:
Democrat Mary Peltola was declared the victor in Alaska's Senate race Tuesday, but Justice Department officials say their interest in the contentious campaign has not waned.

A criminal grand jury investigation remains underway into whether Peltola staffers or others recruited a spoiler candidate with a similar name to incumbent Dan S. Sullivan (R) in an effort to confuse voters - allegations Peltola has denied.

In a parallel civil case, the Justice Department continues to appeal a federal judge's ruling last month denying the agency's extraordinary request to delay certification of the vote over concerns the outcome could be tainted by that potential effort to siphon efforts away from the incumbent.

"The priority of investigating a criminal potential fraud doesn't stop because of the election, no matter who wins or loses," Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters last week.

When asked whether his department would drop those legal battles if Peltola took a significant lead, Blanche added: "No. That investigation remains where it was, which means I'm not going to talk about it."

Still, after a flurry of activity on both legal fronts in the run-up to Election Day, there have been few public signs of progress since the Nov. 3 vote. After the race was called late Tuesday evening, a Justice Department spokesperson said the agency stands by Blanche's earlier remarks.

Peltola has denied any involvement in a scheme to confuse voters. The other Sullivan on the ballot - retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan - has repeatedly maintained his candidacy was legitimate.

He ultimately netted fewer than 5,000 votes, less than half the more than 12,000-vote lead Peltola secured over her Republican opponent.

Democrats have condemned both the civil suit and the criminal investigation as a norm-shattering effort by the Justice Department to influence the election's outcome.

Michael J. Heyman, the U.S. attorney in Alaska, took the unusual step of confirming the existence of the grand jury investigation, which had been underway since the summer, at a news conference five days before the election.

Such probes are typically carried out in secret and Justice Department guidelines typically advise prosecutors from taking investigative steps before an election that could be seen as a sign of political bias.

Though Heyman declined to discuss details of the probe, The Washington Post has reported that prosecutors have issued dozens of subpoenas and sent target letters and document preservation warnings to those it believes might have been involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan.

Among the recipients was Marc Elias, a prominent Democratic voting rights and election lawyer, whose firm represented Peltola's campaign. A lawyer at the firm, whose text messages were quoted in a New York Times story, documenting the alleged recruitment effort also received a target letter, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss details of the ongoing probe.

Elias dismissed those warnings as the latest attempt by the Justice Department to target President Donald Trump's political enemies.

The Justice Department's civil suit was filed just weeks before the vote and as early voting was underway. Department lawyers had asked the court to suspend certification, in the event of a narrow Republican loss, until an investigation could be carried out into whether the outcome had been tainted.

In her Nov. 1 ruling dismissing the case, U.S. District Judge Sharon L. Gleason said she had no authority to order such a probe and noted the department had offered no suggestion as to how such an investigation could be carried out while respecting the secrecy of voters' ballot choices.

The department immediately appealed Gleason's ruling to the San Francisco-based U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, which has so far shown no sign of taking up the matter quickly.

The court has set a briefing schedule for arguments that extends until Jan. 11 - more than a week after Peltola is expected to be sworn in.

The Justice Department has not asked to accelerate that schedule or moved to withdraw its case.

Richard L. Hasen, a prominent election law scholar at UCLA, urged the appellate judges not to let the matter linger in a "friend of the court" brief filed Friday.

"This Court should send a swift and clear message to the federal government and the country," Hasen wrote in the filing, "that the State of Alaska, and Alaska alone, has the right to certify the winner of its elections."

Patrick Marley contributed to this report.
